newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analyst cuts French wheat, barley yield estimates.
newsitem.headline: Analyst cuts French wheat, barley yield estimates.

text.p: Analyst Strategie Grains slightly reduced its estimates for French wheat and barley yields in 1997 to reflect potential damage to crops from prolonged drought.
But the analyst said on Tuesday that with the exception of the southeast, crops may emerge unscathed if the weather breaks in April.
In its monthly report dated April 15 the analyst cut its estimate for French soft wheat yields to seven tonnes per hectare from 7.31 tonnes forecast last month and 7.27 tonnes reached in 1996/97.
It revised barley yields to 6.10 tonnes from 6.19 tonnes last month and 6.19 last year.
It kept its estimate for maize yields unchanged from last month at 8.10 tonnes per hectare. This would represent a drop from 8.36 tonnes last year.
Strategie Grains put 1997/98 soft wheat production at 34.51 million tonnes against 34.69 million last year.
Barley output was seen rising to 9.73 million tonnes from 9.46 million last year but maize production was expected to fall to 13.93 million tonnes from 14.45 million last year.
Stategie Grains said water tables were running low in the grain belt of central France and the Paris basin, a situation similar to last year at the same stage.
But last year record yields in northern France helped offset the poor performance of crops in central France and the Paris basin.
"In the west, centre and in the north, the situation is not dramatic. If it rains in April the plants will not have suffered much," the analyst said.
But in the southeast the drought had now done irreversible damage to crops, the report said.
French weather service Meteo France said last week that the south of France was suffering due to a virtual absence of rain since January 25.
On the positive side fewer regions than last year faced a severe moisture shortfall, the analyst said.
But the lack of rain has limited crops' capacity to absorb fertiliser.
Warm weather since April 7 also threatened to rapidly aggravate the moisture shortfall for crops, the analyst warned.
